chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from al-Idris ibn Abdillah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who reached the people at Jamarat al-Aqaba (Jam'ah), and feared that if he proceeded to 'Arafat, the people would depart from Jam'ah before he reached it. He (AS) said: If he expects that the people will be at Jam'ah before sunrise, let him go to 'Arafat. And if he fears that he will not reach Jam'ah, let him stand at Jam'ah, then depart with the people, and his Hajj is complete.

These two reports indicate that when one is able, standing at 'Arafat is obligatory. And in case of necessity, it is permissible to restrict oneself to al-Mash'ar al-Haram. And it also indicates the obligation of that.

key_terms.الْمَشْعَرِ الْحَرَامِ: al-Mash'ar al-Haram (the Sacred Monument, often referring to Muzdalifah or the stoning site in this context)
key_terms.جَمْعٍ: Jam'ah (Jamarat al-Aqaba, the first stoning site)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a pilgrim misses 'Arafat due to crowds?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani's al-Ishtibār elucidates the principle of *rukhsa* (dispensation) in Hajj rituals, specifically addressing the tension between the obligatory standing at 'Arafat and the practical necessity of avoiding harm or excessive difficulty. It establishes that while 'Arafat is the pillar of Hajj, standing at Jam'ah (often identified with al-Mash'ar al-Haram in this context) suffices if one fears missing the main gathering due to crowd dynamics, reflecting the Shia juristic emphasis on balancing ritual perfection with ease. The concluding note reinforces that this concession is strictly for cases of necessity, preserving the primary obligation for those who are able.
